book: 086 - Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Girls is philosophical because it is stark, raw, and accurate about what is common to human existence: identity, friendship, expectations, and ultimately the meaning of life. It claims Hannah, for all her horribleness (the funeral pitch to her dying editor's widow, doing coke to write truthfully about drugs), follows Socrates's call to know thyself in a millennial register. It then surveys the volume's approaches - existentialism, business ethics, the seven deadly sins, Daoism and Confucianism, Freud, Kristeva - as ways of knowing Hannah, Marnie, Jessa, Shosh, Ray, and Adam, and thereby ourselves.

Frost argues that critics who call Girls unwatchable because Hannah steals the hotel housekeeper's tip and the characters are unlikeable are watching television the wrong way. Using Adorno's 'How to Look at Television,' he shows how mainstream standardized shows (Friends and its copies) pre-digest viewing, how Sex and the City exemplifies Adorno's ideological 'fake-realism,' and how hidden messages of adjustment work through audience identification - none of which Girls permits with its raw sex scenes, Hannah's unglamorous body, and Jessa's non-judged promiscuity. Because identification with Hannah, Marnie, and Jessa (the diary-reading, the request to Laird for heroin) is impossible, Girls escapes the culture industry and exercises the viewer's critical faculties toward the Kantian autonomy and emancipation Adorno demands - which is also why role-model feminist criticism (Catherine Scott's) misses the point.

Robison-Greene defends Girls against the twin criticisms that it is bad feminism (Hannah 'sluttin' around' jokes, Adam's degrading sex with Hannah) and irresponsibly all-white. She argues there is no single correct conception of feminism from which to judge Dunham, that 'demeaning sex is anti-feminist, so portraying it is anti-feminist' is an invalid argument (by analogy with portraying racism in 12 Years a Slave), and notes MacKinnon's dominance view that sex itself may be inherently demeaning only to conclude the debate is legitimate, not settled against the show. On race, she contends Dunham writing authentically from her own half-Jew, half-WASP experience produces better art than tokenism would, and that the obligation to fix representation falls on networks and creators with the relevant experience, not on punishing one writer.

McCrossin asks whether Adam's Season Two finale run across Brooklyn to break down the door of a dangerously unraveling Hannah ('I was always here') is heroic, set against Hannah's 'You don't need to be like a hero' chair-and-mattress scene and Adam's 'I don't want to help... I was doing it because I love you' quarrel. He argues an act is heroic - being an 'Extraordinary Samaritan' like Wesley Autrey, the Subway Samaritan, unlike the trained Sullenberger - only when done on purpose to help, not from obligation, training, or love's compulsion, testing the point with Batman's motives. Since Adam insists no one ever does anything from a want to help, his rescue's heroic status is left genuinely open.

Greene constructs the conditions of a 'legitimate spoiler' - the thing cannot be too old (with never-expiring exceptions like Darth Vader being Luke's father, Snape killing Dumbledore, and the Planet of the Apes reveal), cannot be common knowledge (Anne Boleyn's beheading, the Titanic hitting the iceberg), and must be significant rather than mundane. Applying them, he concludes Girls cannot be conventionally spoiled: nobody 'ships' Hannah and Adam the way audiences shipped Ross and Rachel, because the show's plot turns are mere backdrop for its conversations and meltdowns. The only true way to spoil Girls is to reveal its hilariously written lines in advance.

Blessing and Wezowiczi test theories of life's meaning on the two narcissists of Girls: Hannah, whose purpose-driven pursuit of being a writer (manufacturing experiences, ignoring her father's medical procedure) shows that goal achievement alone collapses into Taylor's and Camus's Sisyphus problem, and Jessa, whose 'life addict' desire-satisfaction illustrates the Nietzschean live-in-the-moment view the authors find reckless and irresponsible. Using Wielenberg's excrement-eater and the subjectivist/objectivist debate, they land on Susan Wolf's 'loving objects that are worthy of love,' then argue via Socrates's examined life and Sartre's bad faith that neither Hannah's phony narrative nor Jessa's protective persona counts as authentic, examined living.

Archibald reads Jessa as Girls' quintessential existentialist: her unbothered abortion ('I'm offended by all the supposed to's'), her 'I am a junkie' honesty, and her refusal to blame her rough past (Sartrean facticity) enact existence precedes essence and Camus's embrace of the absurd. Kierkegaard's 'the crowd is untruth' and 'leveling' explain her contempt for rehab group conformity, while her panic marriage to Thomas-John after Katherine's motherly intervention is diagnosed as bad faith and angst. Her assisting the dying Beadie's suicide attempt - and calling 911 when Beadie recants - becomes the chapter's closing confrontation with Camus's one serious philosophical question, answered by living 'without appeal.'

Addis uses Heidegger to explain why Hannah cannot 'rewrite her world': her enframing habit treats everything and everyone (Laird, Marnie, Adam) only in terms of feeding her 'writer' identity, so her world stays tiny even in vast New York. Heideggerian world, thrownness (Jessa's surprise wedding Shoshanna attends in white, Charlie's departure), and the power of art to de-enframe structure contrasts with Marnie, whose singing - prompted by Ray's question - expands her horizons. Hannah's crying-at-her-desk realization at the ad agency is read as her one genuine acceptance of thrownness, though her enframed self-absorption pulls her back.

Crossley reads the millennials of Girls through Sartre's anguish: Hannah, cut off financially in the pilot, is 'condemned to be free' in a recession that owes her nothing, and Marnie's firing from the gallery ('I don't know what I want... I wish someone would tell me') confronts her with facticity and the terror of self-determination. Marnie's flight into wishing for a moral dictator and her later choice to sing map the bad faith/authenticity distinction, as does Hannah swapping her hoarder-story reading for a pretentious piece on death to please Ray. Even Jessa's total rejection of the 'supposed to's' is outed as its own bad faith, and the ad-agency arc shows twenty-first-century authenticity is inevitably compromised by the need to eat.

Van Loon explains the q-tip scene ('On All Fours') as Kierkegaardian anxiety made flesh: freed by her parents and facing the e-book deadline, Hannah confronts the infinity of possibilities and, like Sartre's vertigo over the cliff, shoves the q-tip into her ear - embracing all possibilities at once and relapsing into bad faith by becoming a victim of fate. Each girl handles freedom differently: Shoshanna remains in an innocence prior to freedom, Jessa jokes her way out of seriousness, Marnie denies her anxiety. Against these, the Season Two FaceTime call to Adam models Kierkegaard's leap of faith and the 'knight of faith' - surrendering, making oneself vulnerable, and accepting that anxiety will return.

Sirvent and Avery take Shoshanna's Listen, Ladies! advice book to ask whether rules can govern romance, contrasting Kantian rule-duty ethics (Ray's dating rules that are 'not commandments') with Bentham-Mill utilitarian calculation (Jessa's 'depends on the virgin'). Kierkegaard and Nietzsche - extended through Žižek's Lacanian 'Big Other' of God, Duty, or Utility - show such impersonal systems let us dodge responsibility: Jessa plays Kierkegaard's aesthete escaping boredom, while Hannah's 'just to be an asshole' boss seduction and the Marnie-Elijah hookup express ressentiment and self-hatred. Their positive proposal is Aristotelian virtue ethics - becoming a certain kind of person - completed by Butler's Undoing Gender: to be ethical you must risk being 'undone by each other,' as Adam demands of Hannah ('You don't wanna know me').

Mahon and Walker rebrand the seven deadly sins for Girls: Self-Absorption as Augustine's 'love of one's own excellence' (Hannah pitching her e-book at her editor's funeral, calling her grandmother 'the old Flo Job... sluttin' around'), Entitlement for Hannah's 'voice of my generation' demands and Marnie's rage at Charlie's success, and Sleeping Around as the John Paul II point about reducing a person to an object of gratification - Adam's fantasy sex with Hannah and his degradation of Natalia. Envy (Hannah on Tally's tragedy), gluttony in drug-fueled relapses (Aquinas's five ways), flakiness as Kant's indolent free-rider who needs others but never helps (Jessa missing her own abortion), and Senecan irritability (Jessa spitting at the Bushwick party, Ray's hatreds, Shoshanna's 'whiny nothings' outburst) complete the survey - redeemed by the girls' stubborn friendship.

Wible asks whether the workplace abuse in Girls - Hannah's two unpaid intern years, the harassment at the law firm, the 30-day e-book deadline that triggers her OCD, Marnie hostessing at a gentlemen's club - is defensible by young workers' inexperience and the 'experience paradox.' Against the boot-camp defense he argues from the meaning of work (Gini's 'I work, therefore I am,' Schumacher's good work) and from Marx on alienation from the products of labor, but his core standard is Kant's: persons must be treated as ends, never merely as means, which the editor who wants the book and not the person violates. He concludes that young workers' vulnerability (no savings, no leverage, reluctance to blow the whistle) warrants paid internships, transparency, and two-way respect.

Ketcham sets Hannah B (Brooklyn) beside an imagined Hannah D (a Darfur village terrorized by the Janjaweed) to ask whether personal fulfillment depends on culture or on the individual. Rejecting relativism (which, per Alford, cannot even condemn suppression of belief), he turns to Rawls's Law of Peoples - five minimal human rights any well-ordered society must grant - and builds a thought experiment, 'Blandland,' a minimally compliant country where both Hannahs relocate. His conclusion: even Rawlsian minimum rights, under which life can remain Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short,' plus personal drive and the attitudes of others, jointly and indeterminately decide what either Hannah can become.

Fisher explains the show's cycle - the girls want someone only while that person rejects them - through psychoanalytic theories of desire. Freud supplies the id/ego/superego machinery (cocaine-era Hannah dancing to 'I Don't Care (I Love It)' as pure id; Dunham's body-critical audience as the superego), while Lacan's desire - the 'untold' that must be named (Hannah's bedroom kink questions to Eric), drive, and jouissance beyond the pleasure principle - shows desire circling its object and never being satisfied, as when Hannah's e-book deal collapses into her worst OCD episode. Žižek's objet a as the object-cause of desire reads Marnie loving Charlie only once he is over her: desire reproduces itself rather than reaching its goal.

Keszeg first maps Sex and the City's four women onto classic fashion theories - Barthes's fashion system for Carrie, Carlyle's clothing morality for Samantha, Spencer's evolutionary equity for Charlotte, Veblen and Simmel's status signaling for Miranda - then argues Girls' four break these inherited codes. Marnie's perfectly status-calibrated outfits fall into 'complete freefall' with her life; Jessa wears bohemian otherness (Yves Saint-Laurent, 'Down with the Ritz - long live the street'); Shoshanna embodies the Kierkegaardian aesthetic stage of shifting, consequence-free equivocation ('I think it's time to unchoose some of those choices'); and Hannah's one-piece pyjamas, worn outside, invent a 'sophomoric dress' that negates the fashion system entirely - the generational attitude (via Mannheim) the show both celebrates and satirizes.

Adleberg asks whether Jessa is right that she is not 'the ladies.' Against Shoshanna's common-sense biological determinism and pop-neuroscience like Brizendine's 'male brain' (refuted via brain plasticity and Fausto-Sterling), she deploys Butler's point that identity categories are always normative and exclusionary (Marnie's 'that's what men do' to Charlie) and Beauvoir's and Spelman's social constructionism - mothers already treating infants differently - to show gender is made, not born. With Haslanger's call to resist unjust gender meanings, she concludes that neither conforming (Marnie craving dominant Booth Jonathan) nor defying stereotypes (Jessa's bathroom sex, 'what if I want to feel like I have udders?') should be compulsory; only objectifying harm, as with Adam and Natalia, is wrong.

Zurba reads all four girls through Julia Kristeva's adolescent malady: the faith that 'there certainly can not not be an absolutely satisfying other,' which curdles into a 'kamikaze syndrome' of nihilism and self-destruction when the ideal love object disappoints. Hannah's idealized Adam ('too absent, too present or too weird') fails her, producing self-deprecating sex, compulsive counting, and the q-tip collapse; Marnie's disappointment becomes boredom and cruelty toward Hannah; Jessa's absent father leaves her 'swimming without a life vest' on heroin; Shoshanna invests hers in Sex and the City pastiche yet alone learns to love Ray as he is. Following Kristeva (and Freud) the cure is not the perfect partner but love as psychic openness, imagination, and treating the self as 'a work in progress.'

LaRocca asks what the liberal arts (Dunham's Oberlin, the girls' rural-college degrees) are for, reading Girls through the Greek notion of paideia: Plato's discussions of whether virtue can be taught (Protagoras), rhetoric as a mere 'knack' versus care of the soul (Gorgias), and education as becoming human (Republic), joined to Isocrates's 'development of judgment' as the father of liberal education. Against contemporary self-expression-and-selfie culture, he holds that the self is constituted outer-directed - Hannah's mentorship of her traumatized cousin Rebecca being the show's clinic in empathy - and he uses the agon (Honig, Mouffe) to recast the Beach House blowup as contest over whether the others are 'worthy' opponents. Dunham-as-doppelganger (like Plato's Socrates, like Kaufman in Adaptation) makes the show itself a work of paideia and a criticism of modern academic humanism, with Aristotle's Poetics invoked for drama's basis in conflict.

Carleo and D'Ambrosio read Hannah's 'busy trying to become who I am' through the classical Chinese debate over names: her self-claimed title 'writer' preceding any conduct is the Confucian nightmare of names divorced from actuality, diagnosed by the Analects's rectification of names ('rulers should rule, fathers should father') and the sheep-stealing passage warning against over-identifying with a single role. Adam, by contrast, lives the Daoist ideal - the empty vessel of the Daodejing acting by wu wei, and Zhuangzi's butterfly dream fluidity in his role-play sex and absorbed woodworking, unattached to titles. Mencius and Xunzi frame the resolution: by Season Three Hannah finally rectifies names at GQ while Adam's non-identity turns delusional, vindicating the ideal of being an 'internal sage and external king' - Daoist in private, responsible to roles in public.

holes.name: Lacanian Desire (jouissance and objet a)
holes.what: Lacan's theory that desire is insatiable - a drive circling its object rather than reaching it, sustained by objet a as object-cause and jouissance beyond the pleasure principle.
holes.why: Chapter 27's entire account of the Girls romance cycle rests on Lacan's theory of desire, which taxonomy.json's other Lacan slugs (mirror stage; the RSI registers) do not cover.

holes.name: Fashion Theory (clothes as sign system)
holes.what: The line of theory from Carlyle's Sartor Resartus through Barthes's fashion system and Veblen/Simmel's status signaling that treats clothing as a code expressing morality, sexuality, and social position.
holes.why: Chapter 28 interprets each Girls character's wardrobe entirely through these fashion theories, none of which taxonomy.json contains.

holes.name: Julia Kristeva
holes.what: Psychoanalyst-philosopher of the 'new maladies of the soul': adolescent idealization of love, the need to believe, and the nihilistic 'kamikaze syndrome' when ideals fail.
holes.why: Chapter 30's reading of all four girls as Kristevan adolescents suffering for want of love is built on her Tales of Love, New Maladies of the Soul, and This Incredible Need to Believe, and she is absent from taxonomy.json.

holes.name: Paideia (Greek education of the soul)
holes.what: The classical Greek ideal of education as the formation of the whole person for life in the polis, debated by Plato and codified for the liberal arts by Isocrates.
holes.why: Chapter 31 evaluates the girls' liberal-arts education against paideia specifically, a concept taxonomy.json lacks despite its Plato and Aristotle entries.

holes.name: Agonism (affirmation of perpetual contest)
holes.what: The view (Honig, Mouffe) that conflict and contest are perpetual and valuable, demanding respect for worthy opponents rather than resolution or consensus.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses the agon to reinterpret the show's conflicts (the Beach House fight, MFA vs NYC) as worthy contest, and taxonomy.json has no slug for agonistic thought.
